Model fit — actuals vs out-of-fold predictions

The model is official data climatology plus a calibrated blend of the satellite index and a within-season carry term, refit with each safra held out. The 80% interval is honest: it covers 83% of held-out fortnights.

Audit (Aug 26): mills that opened or idled mid-period (6 + 5 of 153) offset at fleet level and are now masked per mill-year; the audit also removed a look-ahead in the standardisation — the deployable index uses only trailing history (live-faithful) and scores better: MAE 2.91 Mt, corr 0.56, 88% direction on big anomalies (2019+, out-of-fold). Survivorship of mills that closed before 2026 remains a known limit of the early-year index.
Positioning: the model does not out-forecast human consensus in normal fortnights — its edge is direction on abnormal fortnights (76–78% sign accuracy on top-tercile anomalies) and availability: it updates ~2 days after a fortnight closes, consensus or no consensus, publication or no publication.

The 2026/27 season and the live forecast

UNICA’s fortnightly series stopped at 2H June (released Aug 6, five weeks late). The satellite index flagged the 2H June collapse (official 31.0 Mt, z = −2.2) with its most negative reading of the season — computable five weeks before that print. July exists only as a monthly total via the agriculture ministry; August is published nowhere.

July scored the model honestly: actual 96.5 Mt vs 89.2 forecast — the carry term over-extrapolated the June crash while the satellite read July as near-normal. Lesson logged: when satellite and carry disagree after a one-fortnight shock, trust the satellite’s reversion. August (revised with July in the carry): ≈ 91 Mt, −7.5% YoY.

The satellite index against the crush record

The index is the fleet mean of per-scene boiler-core thermal anomalies (top-70 pixels per mill, ~6 ha), each z-scored within its mill’s own calendar-month history — a year-over-year activity anomaly with no official inputs at all.

4

How a mill becomes a number

No labels, no supervision: the method finds each mill’s boiler block from its own history and measures it against the same scene it appears in. Everything downstream of the raw pixels is a fixed rule, so the index is reproducible from the archive and identical live and in backtest.

Why each step exists. The in-scene differential is the load-bearing trick: sun, season and airmass move the whole box together, so subtracting the same scene’s median leaves process heat. The core is fixed rather than “hottest pixels today” because at many sites the hottest surface off-season is sun-baked ground elsewhere in the box — the case study below shows exactly that. The z-cell is (mill, calendar month) so a June reading is only ever compared with that mill’s other Junes, and it is trailing-only (≥8 prior scenes) so the live number never peeks at the future — the flattering look-ahead version scored r 0.70 vs the honest 0.54, and we ship the honest one. ON/OFF is not a hard classifier at fleet level: single scenes have SNR ≈ 1, so the design is many mills × many scenes, and conviction comes from the aggregate.

6

Instrument update — ECOSTRESS night passes added

The index now fuses two instruments: Landsat’s constant 10:30 day pass and ECOSTRESS’s night passes from the ISS (70 m, ~half of all overpasses at night). Each source is z-scored against its own (mill, month, day/night) history, then pooled — scale-free, so no cross-calibration is needed.

Deployable index, 2019+Fortnight corrModel MAE (Mt)Anomaly corrSkill vs clim.
Landsat only0.463.070.53+22%
Landsat + ECOSTRESS night (18,900 scenes, 152 mills)0.472.930.55+25%
Two honest findings from the fusion study. Night passes help the model, not the correlation: at 152 mills the index is validity-limited, not noise-limited, so the extra scenes buy a ~5% MAE improvement and 60% more observations per fortnight (blackout resilience) rather than a higher r — at a 5-mill pilot the same fusion moved r from 0.30 to 0.38, exactly as the scaling law predicts. ECOSTRESS day passes are excluded: their overpass hour drifts across 06:00–18:00, and the changing solar geometry swamps the thermal differential (r = 0.09 alone). The method needs constant conditions — a fixed morning hour, or night — not daylight per se.
